title: Le Chatelier's Principle

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part II, Class 11 — Equilibrium

summary: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed (by a change in concentration, pressure, volume, or temperature), the equilibrium shifts in the direction that partially counteracts the disturbance.
explanation: This is a qualitative predictive tool, not a mathematical formula: increasing a reactant's concentration shifts equilibrium toward products (to consume some of the excess); increasing pressure/decreasing volume shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles; increasing temperature shifts equilibrium in the endothermic direction (since that direction absorbs some of the added heat). A catalyst, notably, does NOT shift equilibrium position at all — it speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, only helping equilibrium be reached faster.
commonMisconceptions: Believing a catalyst shifts equilibrium toward products — a catalyst only speeds up reaching the SAME equilibrium position, it never changes where that position is.

Forgetting that pressure/volume changes only affect equilibrium position when the number of gas moles differs between reactant and product sides — if moles are equal on both sides, changing pressure has no shifting effect.
examples: In the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃), increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward ammonia, since the product side has fewer gas moles (2 vs 4).
genZNote: Le Chatelier's principle is chemistry's version of 'whatever you throw at me, I'll push back a little' — equilibrium always leans against the disturbance.
searchKeywords: effect of pressure temperature on equilibrium
